summary: Defines Per-Domain Behaviors for Differentiated Services and sets out the format and procedure for proposing new ones to the working group. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3086 explains how to describe the treatment a group of packets receives while crossing a Differentiated Services domain. It provides a required format for PDB specifications and an example for Best Effort traffic.

questions: what is a diffserv per domain behavior
what is a per domain behavior
what is the best effort pdb
subtitle: A definition and specification template for edge-to-edge Diffserv behavior.

tldr.problem: Diffserv defines how individual routers forward packets, but service designers also need a way to describe the treatment a traffic group receives across an entire domain.
tldr.mechanism: A Per-Domain Behavior (PDB) combines edge classification and traffic conditioning with one or more per-hop behaviors inside a domain. The memo defines the attributes and sections required to specify a PDB.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3086 defines PDB terminology, a specification format and a reference Best Effort PDB. It is an Informational memo.

today: RFC 3086 is an Informational memo defining Per-Domain Behaviors and a format for specifying them. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What a Per-Domain Behavior Describes
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (Diffserv) uses codepoints in IP headers to select packet treatment. The framework defined per-hop behaviors (PHBs) for routers; this memo adds the Per-Domain Behavior (PDB) to describe expected treatment from one edge of a Diffserv domain to another.

A PDB is associated with a PHB or list of PHBs and traffic-conditioning requirements. Its measurable attributes describe what happens to a target group of packets. The memo distinguishes this technical building block from a customer-facing service or agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: A PHB describes what happens to packets at a router. A PDB describes the expected treatment of a selected packet group across a whole network domain.

sections.title: Edge Conditioning and Domain Transit
sections.content:
A classifier selects the target packets at the domain edge. Traffic conditioning, which may include marking, shaping or policing, forms a traffic aggregate and marks conforming packets for the PHB associated with the PDB. The PDB also describes the treatment packets receive as they cross the domain.

The PDB attributes must account for traffic aggregates splitting and merging along different paths. A PDB does not have to apply to every possible topology, but its limits must be stated. If packets need to be remarked inside the domain, that point should be treated as a domain boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain edge selects and conditions packets before marking them for a PHB. The PDB describes their treatment inside the domain, including any limits caused by its topology.

sections.title: Required PDB Specification Sections
sections.content:
Every PDB specification must include an applicability statement; technical specification; attributes; parameters; assumptions; example uses; environmental concerns; and security considerations. The technical section identifies classification, traffic conditioning and PHBs, while attributes describe measurable behavior such as delay, throughput or packet loss.

Attributes must be explicit and quantifiable, and the specification must explain how measurements are made and characteristics derived. Assumptions such as lossless links or stable routing must be stated. Parameters may describe network-specific limits such as hop count, bandwidth or entry and exit points.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDB specification must say what it applies to, how to configure it, what behavior it claims and which assumptions it relies on. It must also cover examples, network constraints and security.

sections.title: Measuring PDB Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes long-term behavior, such as throughput measured over a stated period, from short-term behavior such as burst size and packets that may queue at once. The second kind matters for buffer needs and loss.

Topology and traffic aggregation can change the burstiness and loss of a traffic aggregate. A specification must state the conditions under which its attributes hold, including any routing or resource assumptions that affect them.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDB needs measurements for both average traffic and short bursts. Its specification must explain when those measurements are expected to hold.

sections.title: Best Effort and Review Process
sections.content:
The memo defines Best Effort as a reference PDB for normal Internet traffic that needs no special differentiation. It uses the Default PHB, requires no traffic conditioning beyond the ingress-link limit and has no defined bounds for delay, availability or loss. Its stated attribute is that packets get resources when they are available and are not completely starved.

A proposed PDB should use the template and include deployment experience with measured results or convincing simulation results. If a Diffserv working group is active, a review panel examines its claimed characteristics before working-group last call. The expected review period is 4 to 8 weeks.
sections.plainLanguage: Best Effort is the reference behavior for traffic that has no special requirements. A proposed PDB should include evidence from deployment or simulation and undergo review.
